name: OPT4 Chapter 5: Identity and Access Management (Domain 5)

questions.stem: Henry uses his organizationally provided credentials to log into his workstation and is then able to use services across the organization and in the cloud. What identity solution has his organization implemented?
questions.explanation: Single sign-on provides a single authentication process to allow authorization to multiple services. An access control list, or ACL, is a ruleset used to determine if a subject can gain access to a service or system. Multifactor requires multiple factors, and the specifics of how Henry logged in were not discussed in the question. Finally, role-based access control uses a subject's role(s) to determine if they can access a service or system, and no mention of roles was made.
optionNotes: Incorrect. An ACL is a ruleset deciding whether a subject may access a particular object or system. It doesn't let one login carry over to many services.
Correct. Single sign-on means one authentication event (logging into the workstation) gives Henry authorized access to multiple services across the organization and the cloud.
Incorrect. MFA means using multiple types of authentication factors. The question never describes how Henry authenticated, only that one login reached many services.
Incorrect. RBAC grants access based on a subject's assigned roles. The scenario never mentions roles, and RBAC is an authorization model, not a single-login solution.

questions.stem: Jim's organization-wide implementation of IDaaS offers broad support for cloud-based applications. Jim's company does not have internal identity management staff and does not use centralized identity services. Instead, they rely upon Active Directory for AAA services. Which of the following options should Jim recommend to best handle the company's on-site identity needs?
options: Use an on-premises third-party identity service.
Design an internal solution to handle the organization's unique needs.
questions.explanation: Since Jim's organization is using a cloud-based identity as a service solution, a third-party, on-premises identity service can provide the ability to integrate with the IDaaS solution, and the company's use of Active Directory is widely supported by third-party vendors. OAuth is used to log in to third-party websites using existing credentials and would not meet the needs described. SAML is a markup language and would not meet the full set of AAA needs. Since the organization is using Active Directory, a custom in-house solution is unlikely to be as effective as a preexisting third-party solution and may take far more time and expense to implement.
optionNotes: Incorrect. OAuth is an authorization framework that lets users sign in to third-party websites with existing credentials. It doesn't give on-site systems the full set of identity and AAA services they need.

Correct. An on-premises third-party identity service can integrate with the cloud IDaaS solution, and third-party vendors widely support Active Directory. That makes it a good fit for a company with no internal identity staff.
Incorrect. SAML is an XML-based markup language for exchanging authentication and authorization assertions. On its own it doesn't cover all of the company's on-site AAA needs.

Incorrect. A custom in-house solution would likely work worse than an existing third-party product that already supports Active Directory. It would also cost more and take longer, especially with no identity staff.

questions.stem: What role does a policy enforcement point play in a zero trust environment?
options: It makes decisions for the policy engine.
It is the workstation or mobile device used by the end user.
It deploys role-based access controls based on local policy.
It receives authorization requests and sends them to the policy decision point.
questions.explanation: A policy enforcement point in a zero trust environment receives authorization requests and then sends them to the policy decision point. They are used anywhere that authorization controls are needed. They do not make decisions for the policy engine, can exist beyond workstations and mobile devices, and use policies set at the zero trust control layer rather than just at the endpoint device.
optionNotes: Incorrect. The PEP doesn't make decisions for the policy engine. Decisions come from the policy decision point (the policy engine plus the policy administrator), and the PEP only carries them out.
Incorrect. The user's workstation or mobile device is the subject or endpoint asking for access. PEPs are placed wherever authorization controls are needed, not only on end-user devices.
Incorrect. PEPs apply policies set centrally at the zero trust control layer, not local endpoint policies, and they don't set up RBAC on their own.
Correct. The PEP takes in authorization requests, passes them to the policy decision point, and then enforces the decision by allowing or blocking the connection to the resource.

questions.stem: Voice pattern recognition is what type of authentication factor?
questions.explanation: Voice pattern recognition is “something you are,” a biometric authentication factor, because it measures a physical characteristic of the individual authenticating.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Something you know covers secrets you've memorized, like passwords or PINs. Voice recognition checks how you sound, not what you know, so it isn't a knowledge factor.
Incorrect. Something you have means a physical object the user carries, such as a smartcard, hardware token or authenticator app on a phone. Your voice isn't an object you possess.
Correct. Voice pattern recognition is a biometric: it measures a physical characteristic of the person, so it is a 'something you are' (Type 3) factor.
Incorrect. Somewhere you are is a location-based factor, using things like GPS or IP address. Voice recognition measures the person, not where they are.

questions.stem: If Susan's organization requires her to log in with her username, a PIN, a password, and a retina scan, how many distinct authentication factor types has she used?
questions.explanation: Susan has used two distinct types of factors: the PIN and password are both Type 1 factors, and the retina scan is a Type 3 factor. Her username is not a factor.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Too few. The PIN and password count as one factor type (something you know), but the retina scan is a separate Type 3 factor (something you are), which makes two types.
Correct. The PIN and password are both Type 1 (something you know) and the retina scan is Type 3 (something you are). The username only identifies her and is not an authentication factor.
Incorrect. This answer counts the PIN and password as separate factors. Both are something you know, so together they add no new factor type, and the username is identification, not authentication.
Incorrect. This answer counts every item as its own factor. The username is only an identity claim, and the PIN and password share the something-you-know type, so only two distinct types are used.

questions.stem: Charles wants to deploy a credential management system (CMS). He wants to keep the keys as secure as possible. Which of the following is the best design option for his CMS implementation?
questions.explanation: Hardware Security Modules, or HSMs, are the most secure way to store keys associated with a CMS. They provide enhanced key management capabilities and are often required to be FIPS certified. In addition to these advantages, an HSM can improve cryptographic performance for the organization due to dedicated hardware designed for just that purpose. Long keys and using AES-256 are good practices, but an HSM provides greater security and will require appropriate cryptographic controls already. Changing passphrases can be challenging across an organization; instead, securing the passphrases and keys is more important and reasonable for most organizations.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Picking AES-256 over 3DES is a sound algorithm choice, but it only makes the encryption stronger. It does nothing to protect how the keys are stored, and an HSM gives the CMS more security than an algorithm choice can.

Incorrect. Long keys make brute-force attacks harder. They don't protect the stored keys from theft or misuse, though. The book says an HSM gives more security and already requires appropriate cryptographic controls.

Correct. An HSM is the most secure place to store CMS keys. It is dedicated, tamper-resistant hardware, often FIPS certified, that adds stronger key management and can also speed up cryptographic operations.

Incorrect. Changing passphrases regularly is hard to manage across an organization. The book says securing the passphrases and keys themselves matters more and is more practical than frequent changes.

questions.stem: Brian is a researcher at a major university. As part of his research, he logs into a computing cluster hosted at another institution using his own university's credentials. Once logged in, he is able to access the cluster and use resources based on his role in a research project, as well as using resources and services in his home organization. What has Brian's home university implemented to make this happen?
questions.explanation: Brian's organization is using a federated identity management approach where multiple organizations allow identities to be used across the organizations. Each organization needs to conduct identity proofing of their own staff members' identities and provide them with rights and role information that will allow them to use resources within the federated identity environment.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Domain stacking isn't a recognized identity management model. Letting a user log in at another institution with home credentials requires a federation agreement to share identity information.

Correct. In federated identity management, several organizations agree to trust each other's identities. Each one proofs its own users and supplies their rights and role information, so Brian's home credentials work on the partner institution's cluster.
Incorrect. Domain nesting isn't a standard CISSP identity concept. It's a distractor that loosely suggests nested trust within one directory, not sharing identities between separate organizations.

Incorrect. Hybrid login isn't a defined identity management model. Cross-organization access with home credentials and role-based rights is federation. A 'hybrid' setup usually means mixing on-premises and cloud identity inside one organization.

questions.stem: When Sally attempts to authenticate to her organization's services, she knows that the organization uses a mobile device management tool to check her location and whether she's logging in from her company-issued mobile device. What type of authentication is this?
questions.explanation: Authentication that takes attributes such as location, device, and time of day into account is context-aware authentication. This allows organizations to make choices about whether the authentication is appropriate and allowed in addition to the use of credentials. The decision is based on contextual information, not user knowledge or identity factors, which are used only to authenticate. Zero trust may leverage context information, but context-aware authentication alone does not indicate zero trust.
optionNotes: Correct. Context-aware authentication looks at attributes such as location, device, and time of day to decide whether a login is allowed, on top of normal credentials. That matches the MDM checks in this scenario.
Incorrect. Knowledge-based authentication depends on something the user knows, like a password or security questions. Checking location and device uses contextual data, not anything Sally knows.

Incorrect. 'Identity factoring' isn't a standard authentication type. Identity or authentication factors only verify who the user is, while this decision is based on context such as location and device.
Incorrect. Zero trust is a broader architecture that may use contextual information. However, context-aware checks alone don't show that zero trust is in place.

questions.stem: What major issue often results from decentralized access control?
questions.explanation: Decentralized access control can result in less consistency because the individuals tasked with control may interpret policies and requirements differently and may perform their roles in different ways. Access outages, overly granular control, and training costs may occur, depending on specific implementations, but they are not commonly identified issues with decentralized access control.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Access outages can happen under some implementations, but the book says they aren't a commonly identified problem with decentralized access control. Inconsistency is the typical issue.
Correct. When control is decentralized, different people interpret policies and requirements differently and do their jobs in different ways. The result is inconsistent access control.
Incorrect. How granular control is depends on the specific implementation, not on whether administration is decentralized. The book says it's not a typical drawback.
Incorrect. Training costs can be high in some setups, but the book says they aren't the commonly identified problem with decentralized access control.

questions.stem: Callback to a landline phone number is an example of what type of factor?
questions.explanation: A callback to a landline phone number is an example of a “somewhere you are” factor because of the fixed physical location of a wired phone. A callback to a mobile phone would be a “something you have” factor.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Something you know is a memorized secret like a password or PIN. A callback checks where the user is, not what they remember.
Correct. This is correct. A landline is wired to a fixed physical place, so a callback to it confirms the user's location. That makes it a 'somewhere you are' factor.
Incorrect. A callback to a mobile phone would count as something you have, because the phone is a portable device. A landline is tied to a location instead.
Incorrect. Something you are means biometrics, such as fingerprints or iris scans. A phone callback does not measure any physical trait of the user.

questions.stem: What common behavior drives the NIST recommendation that passwords should not expire?
options: Attackers would not have enough time to compromise passwords if they expired.
Users often make minimal changes to passwords to handle change requirements.
Password expiration leads to too little support overhead.
Re-hashing passwords when changes are required is computationally intensive.
questions.explanation: The NIST recommendation to not expire passwords recognizes that users often make minimal changes to their passwords when they are required to change them. In addition, password changes drive significant support overhead as users forget their passwords or otherwise face challenges with them. Longer password lives do create the potential for attackers to have longer to compromise them, but modern password recommendations look for multifactor authentication, which means a compromised password is less of a threat. Hashing new passwords does require computation, but not a significant amount using modern hardware.
optionNotes: Incorrect. This gets it backwards. Expiration limits how long a stolen password stays useful, so it isn't why NIST drops expiration. NIST relies on MFA to reduce the risk of a compromised password instead.

Correct. When forced to change passwords, users tend to make small, predictable tweaks (e.g., incrementing a digit). That adds little security, so NIST SP 800-63B recommends against routine expiration.
Incorrect. This is the reverse of what happens. Forced password changes create a lot of support overhead because users forget new passwords, which is another reason NIST dislikes expiration.
Incorrect. Hashing a new password takes very little computing power on modern hardware, so the cost of re-hashing is not what drives NIST's guidance.

questions.stem: What three functions make up the AAA model?
questions.explanation: AAA refers to a set of security protocols that are used to identify and authorize users and record their activities. The acronym stands for authentication, authorization, and accounting.
optionNotes: Incorrect. This lists access control itself as one of the three, but AAA is the set of functions that make up access control. It keeps authentication and authorization and leaves out accounting, the audit trail of user activity.
Incorrect. Access and administration are not AAA functions. The model is authenticating subjects, authorizing their actions, and accounting for activity through audit trails.
Correct. AAA stands for authentication (identifying users), authorization (granting their permissions), and accounting (recording what they do).
Incorrect. Only accounting belongs to AAA. Auditing is sometimes swapped in for accounting, but assessment is never part of the model, and this option leaves out authentication and authorization.

questions.stem: What directory-based technology underlies Microsoft Active Directory single sign-on?
questions.explanation: Active Directory relies on the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) as part of its single sign-on (SSO) implementation. Zero trust is not a SSO implementation, and Shibboleth is an open-source identity management system. RADIUS is not a single sign-on implementation, although some vendors use it behind the scenes to provide authentication for proprietary SSO.
optionNotes: Correct. Active Directory is built on LDAP, the directory protocol it uses as part of its single sign-on implementation.
Incorrect. Zero trust is a security model that assumes no implicit trust and verifies every access request. It is not a directory technology and not an SSO implementation.
Incorrect. Shibboleth is an open-source, SAML-based federated identity management system. Active Directory SSO is not built on it.
Incorrect. RADIUS is an AAA protocol for authenticating remote and network access, not a directory or an SSO implementation. Some vendors do use it behind the scenes in proprietary SSO products.

questions.stem: Sameer's organization needs to perform identity proofing for new customers. What type of authentication is best suited to identity proofing in this scenario?
questions.explanation: Knowledge-based authentication relies on information that only the individual who wants to prove their identity is likely to know. This might include a mortgage payment amount, vehicle information, or driver's license number among many options. Cognitive passwords, or security questions, are created by users, which means they aren't suited to this type of identity proofing. Palm scans and USB tokens both require prior engagement with the user as well and thus aren't suited for identity proofing with users who are new customers.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Cognitive passwords (security questions) are answers the user sets up in advance. A brand-new customer has never registered any, so they can't be used to prove identity at onboarding.

Correct. Knowledge-based authentication asks about facts only the real person is likely to know, such as a mortgage payment, vehicle details or a driver's license number. These come from outside records, so it works for new customers who have no prior relationship with the organization.
Incorrect. A palm scan only works after the user's biometric template has been enrolled. That means prior engagement with the user is required, which a new customer doesn't have.
Incorrect. USB tokens have to be issued to the user and registered first. That requires an existing relationship, so they can't verify the identity of a new customer.

questions.stem: What type of access controls allow the owner of a file to grant other users access to it using an access control list?
questions.explanation: When the owner of a file makes the decisions about who has rights or access privileges to it, they are using discretionary access control. Role-based access controls would grant access based on a subject's role, while rule-based controls would base the decision on a set of rules or requirements. Nondiscretionary access controls apply a fixed set of rules to an environment to manage access. Nondiscretionary access controls include rule-, role-, and lattice-based access controls.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Role-based access control grants access according to the subject's assigned role or job function, not because a file owner decides who gets in through an ACL.

Incorrect. Nondiscretionary access control applies a fixed set of rules across the whole environment, which means owners can't hand out access at their own discretion. It includes rule-based, role-based and lattice-based models.
Incorrect. Rule-based access control decides access from a set of rules or requirements, such as firewall rules, that apply to everyone. It does not let an owner choose who gets access.
Correct. Under discretionary access control (DAC), the owner of a file decides who has rights to it, usually by editing the file's access control list.

questions.stem: Alex's job requires him to see protected health information (PHI) to ensure proper treatment of patients. His access to their medical records does not provide access to patient addresses or billing information. What access control concept best describes this control?
questions.explanation: Need to know is applied when subjects like Alex have access to only the data they need to accomplish their job. Separation of duties is used to limit fraud and abuse by having multiple employees perform parts of a task. Constrained interfaces restrict what a user can see or do and would be a reasonable answer if need to know did not describe his access more completely in this scenario. Context-dependent control relies on the activity being performed to apply controls, and this question does not specify a workflow or process.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Separation of duties splits a task among several employees to limit fraud and abuse. Alex isn't sharing a task with anyone here; his data access is just being limited.
Incorrect. Constrained interfaces limit what a user can see or do in an application. That would be a reasonable answer, but need to know describes Alex's job-based access more completely.
Incorrect. Context-dependent control applies controls based on the activity or workflow step being performed. The scenario doesn't describe any workflow or process.
Correct. Need to know gives Alex only the data his job requires (PHI for treatment) and keeps addresses and billing information out of his reach.

Ifemoa wants to ensure that users in her organization cannot change their password to a previously used password. What setting should she configure?
questions.explanation: Password history tracks what passwords have been set previously and will not allow reuse. A specific number of past passwords is typically set, and passwords themselves should not be retained. Instead, properly secured hashes are retained and compared to hashes of the new passwords. Length, maximum age, and MFA do not solve the issue of password reuse.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Password length sets how many characters a password must have, which makes it harder to guess. It does nothing to stop a user from setting a password they used before.
Incorrect. Maximum password age forces users to change their password after a set time. It doesn't block reuse, so a user could switch back to an old password.
Incorrect. MFA requires a second authentication factor at login. It adds security but has no effect on which passwords a user is allowed to choose.
Correct. Password history keeps secure hashes of a set number of previous passwords and rejects a new password whose hash matches one of them, which prevents reuse.

questions.stem:
For questions 17–19, please use your knowledge of password policies and their application.

With a password history set, Ifeoma wants to prevent users from resetting their password multiple times to allow them to return to their original password. What setting should she apply?
questions.explanation: Ifeoma knows that a minimum password age of one day will discourage users from resetting their passwords to attempt to return to their original password. Length and complexity do not prevent this if the original password met these requirements, and a maximum age is set in organizations that require password changes on a recurring basis.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Complexity rules control which characters a password must contain. If the original password already met those rules, the user can still cycle back to it, so complexity doesn't stop the reset trick.
Incorrect. Maximum password age makes users change passwords on a regular schedule. It does nothing to stop several quick changes in a row that work through the history list.
Correct. A minimum password age, such as one day, stops users from changing their password over and over in one sitting to push the original out of the history list and reuse it.
Incorrect. Length requirements only set how long a password must be. If the original password was long enough, the user can still return to it after cycling through new passwords.
