With her organization's password behavior under control, Ifeoma wants to ensure that a lost password will not result in easy compromise of her company's accounts. Which of the following controls provides the best protection against password loss or exposure-related compromise?
questions.explanation: Requiring multifactor authentication (MFA) is a common security measure used to prevent unauthorized access to an account in case of password loss or exposure. SSO allows the use of an account throughout systems or services. Federation connects different organizations together, allowing the use of credentials between trusted partners, and password rotation can help, but lost passwords remain dangerous until the rotation happens allowing days, weeks, or even months of potential vulnerable time.
optionNotes: Correct. MFA requires another factor besides the password, such as a token or biometric. A lost or exposed password alone is no longer enough to get into the account.
Incorrect. SSO lets one account work across many systems or services. It does nothing to protect a lost password, and it can actually widen what that password exposes.
Incorrect. Federation lets trusted partner organizations accept each other's credentials. It is about trust between organizations, not about stopping someone from using a stolen password.
Incorrect. Rotation helps some, but a lost password stays usable until the next change. That can leave days, weeks, or even months of exposure.

questions.stem: Jacob is planning his organization's biometric authentication system and is considering retina scans. What concern may be raised about retina scans by others in his organization?
options: Retina scans can reveal information about medical conditions.
Retina scans are painful because they require a puff of air in the user's eye.
Retina scanners are the most expensive type of biometric device.
Retina scanners have a high false positive rate and will cause support issues.
questions.explanation: Retina scans can reveal additional information, including high blood pressure and pregnancy, causing privacy concerns. Newer retina scans don't require a puff of air, and retina scanners are not the most expensive biometric factor. Their false positive rate can typically be adjusted in software, allowing administrators to adjust their acceptance rate as needed to balance usability and security.
optionNotes: Correct. Retina scans image the blood vessel pattern at the back of the eye, which can reveal conditions such as high blood pressure or pregnancy. That raises privacy concerns among employees.
Incorrect. The puff of air is linked to older devices, and newer retina scanners don't use it. Discomfort is not the main concern raised; privacy is.
Incorrect. Retina scanners are not the most expensive type of biometric device, so cost isn't the concern that sets them apart.

Incorrect. Retina scans are among the most accurate biometrics. Their false positive rate can be tuned in software to balance usability and security, so high false positives are not an inherent problem.

questions.stem: Mandatory access control is based on what type of model?
questions.explanation: Mandatory access control systems are based on a lattice-based model. Lattice-based models use a matrix of classification labels to compartmentalize data. Discretionary access models allow object owners to determine access to the objects they control, role-based access controls are often group-based, and rule-based access controls like firewall ACLs apply rules to all subjects they apply to.
optionNotes: Incorrect. In a discretionary model the object owner decides who gets access. MAC is the opposite: the system enforces access based on classification labels, and users can't override it.
Incorrect. Grouping users is typical of role-based access control, where permissions come from group or role membership. MAC instead compares subject clearances against object labels.
Correct. MAC is built on a lattice-based model, which uses a matrix of classification labels to divide data into compartments and set upper and lower access bounds.
Incorrect. Rule-based access control, like firewall ACLs, applies the same global rules to every subject it covers. It doesn't use the classification-label lattice that defines MAC.

questions.stem: Greg wants to control access to iPads used throughout his organization as point-of-sale terminals. Which of the following methods should he use to allow logical access control for the devices in a shared environment?
options: Use a shared PIN for all point-of-sale terminals to make them easier to use.
Use OAuth to allow cloud logins for each user.
Issue a unique PIN to each user for the iPad they are issued.
Use Active Directory and user accounts for logins to the iPads using the AD user ID and password.
questions.explanation: Using an enterprise authentication system like Active Directory that requires individuals to log in with their credentials provides the ability to determine who was logged in if a problem occurs and also allows Greg to quickly and easily remove users who are terminated or switch roles. Using a shared PIN provides no accountability, while unique PINs per user on specifically issued iPads mean that others will not be able to log in. OAuth alone does not provide the services and features Greg needs—it is an authorization service, not an authentication service.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A single shared PIN gives no individual accountability, so nobody can tell who used a terminal when a problem occurs. It also means the PIN has to change for everyone whenever one staff member leaves.
Incorrect. OAuth is an authorization framework, not an authentication service. On its own it doesn't give Greg the centralized user logins and accountability he needs on shared devices.
Incorrect. Tying a unique PIN to the one iPad issued to each user doesn't work when the devices are shared. Other staff couldn't log in to that terminal.

Correct. Enterprise authentication through Active Directory gives each person their own login on any shared iPad, so Greg can see who was logged in. He can also quickly disable users who leave or change roles.

questions.stem: What is the best way to provide accountability for the use of identities?
questions.explanation: Logging systems can provide accountability for identity systems by tracking the actions, changes, and other activities a user or account performs. Authorization does not provide accountability because it validates that a person can perform an action, not who is using the identity. Digital signatures can be used to validate an identity, not to provide accountability by proving who is using it, and Type 1 authentication is something you know. Again, logging is the best way to provide accountability for the use of an identity.
optionNotes: Correct. Logging gives accountability because it records the actions, changes, and other activities each user or account performs, so what was done can be traced back to the identity.
Incorrect. Authorization decides whether an authenticated subject is allowed to perform an action. It does not record or prove what an identity actually did, so it provides no accountability.
Incorrect. Digital signatures can confirm an identity or the origin of a message. They do not keep an ongoing record of what an identity does, so they do not provide accountability for its use.
Incorrect. Type 1 authentication is something you know, such as a password. It proves a claimed identity at login but does not track what that identity does afterward.

questions.stem: Jim has worked in human relations, payroll, and customer service roles in his company over the past few years. What type of process should his company perform to ensure that he has appropriate rights?
questions.explanation: As an employee's role changes, they often experience privilege creep, which is the accumulation of old rights and roles. Account review is the process of reviewing accounts and ensuring that their rights match their owners' role and job requirements. Account revocation removes accounts, while re-provisioning might occur if an employee was terminated and returned or took a leave of absence and returned.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Re-provisioning fits an employee who was terminated and rehired, or who comes back from a leave of absence. Jim has stayed employed and changed roles, so the job is to check the rights he has piled up, not to set up his access again.

Correct. An account review compares an account's rights against its owner's current role and job requirements. That makes it the process that finds and removes access left over from Jim's earlier HR and payroll jobs.
Incorrect. Privilege creep is the problem itself: old rights building up as someone moves between roles. It's what the company needs to fix, not a process the company performs.
Incorrect. Account revocation removes the account entirely, which is appropriate when someone leaves. Jim is still working there and needs access for his current role.

questions.stem: Biba is what type of access control model?
questions.explanation: Biba uses a lattice to control access and is a form of the mandatory access control (MAC) model. It does not use rules, roles, or attributes, nor does it allow user discretion. Users can create content at their level or lower but cannot decide who gets access, levels are not roles, and attributes are not used to make decisions on access control.
optionNotes: Correct. Biba enforces integrity across a lattice of system-assigned levels, so it is a form of mandatory access control. The system decides access, not users.
Incorrect. DAC lets data owners decide who gets access. In Biba, users can create content at their own level or lower, but they cannot choose who accesses it.
Incorrect. RBAC gives permissions to roles or groups based on job function. Biba's integrity levels are lattice levels, not roles.
Incorrect. ABAC uses rules that evaluate multiple attributes. Biba doesn't use attributes to make access decisions. It compares integrity levels within a lattice.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a client-server protocol designed to allow network access servers to authenticate remote users by sending access request messages to a central server?
questions.explanation: RADIUS is an AAA protocol used to provide authentication and authorization; it's often used for modems, wireless networks, and network devices. It uses network access servers to send access requests to central RADIUS servers. Kerberos is a ticket-based authentication protocol; OAuth is an open standard for authentication allowing the use of credentials from one site on third-party sites; and EAP is the Extensible Authentication Protocol, an authentication framework often used for wireless networks.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Kerberos authenticates users with tickets from a KDC. It doesn't have network access servers send access request messages to a central AAA server.
Incorrect. EAP is an authentication framework, often used on wireless networks. It's not a client-server AAA protocol that carries access requests from network access servers to a central server.

Correct. RADIUS is an AAA protocol. Network access servers, such as modem pools, wireless gear and network devices, send access requests to a central RADIUS server for authentication and authorization.
Incorrect. The book describes OAuth as an open standard that lets credentials from one site be used on third-party sites. It isn't used by network access servers to authenticate remote users.

questions.stem: Henry is working with a web application development team on their authentication and authorization process for his company's new application. The team wants to make session IDs as secure as possible. Which of the following is not a best practice that Henry should recommend?
options: The session ID token should be predictable.
The session ID should have at least 64 bits of entropy.
The session length should be at least 128 bits.
The session ID should be meaningless.
questions.explanation: Session identifiers should not be predictable to ensure that attackers can't simply guess or easily brute force session IDS. Web application development best practices currently recommend the use of long session IDs (128 bits or longer) that have sufficient entropy (randomness) to ensure that they will not be easily duplicated or brute-forced. It is also a best practice to make sure the session ID itself is meaningless to prevent information disclosure attacks. Session IDs should expire, however, because a session that never expires could eventually be brute-forced even if all of these recommendations were met.
optionNotes: Correct. Correct choice because this is NOT a best practice. A predictable session ID lets attackers guess or brute-force valid tokens and hijack sessions, so IDs must be unpredictable.
Incorrect. This is a real best practice. Enough entropy (randomness), at least 64 bits, keeps session IDs from being duplicated or brute-forced, so it isn't the answer.
Incorrect. This is a real best practice. Current guidance calls for long session IDs of 128 bits or more to resist brute force, so it isn't the answer.
Incorrect. This is a real best practice. A meaningless ID doesn't encode user or system data, which prevents information disclosure attacks, so it isn't the answer.

questions.stem: Angela uses her smartphone's built-in biometric authentication and an application provided by her employer to log into her account. What type of authentication has she used?
questions.explanation: Passwordless authentication leverages applications and capabilities such as built-in biometric authentication mechanisms. Extended and alternative authentication are not terms used on the exam. The Fast Identity Online Alliance (FIDO) is an open industry association that provides frameworks for passwordless authentication, but SPOT is not a type of passwordless authentication.
optionNotes: Incorrect. "Extended authentication" isn't a recognized authentication category on the exam. Nothing in the scenario points to an extended scheme; the clue is that she logs in without a password.

Correct. Passwordless authentication uses built-in device features like biometrics, along with authenticator apps, so the user can log in without a password. This is what Angela did with her phone and her employer's app.
Incorrect. "Alternative authentication" is not an exam term. It vaguely suggests something other than passwords, but the recognized name for biometric- and app-based login is passwordless.
Incorrect. SPOT is not a type of passwordless authentication. It may be a distractor modeled on FIDO, the industry alliance that publishes frameworks for passwordless authentication.

questions.stem: What type of access control best describes NAC's posture assessment capability?
questions.explanation: The posturing capability of network access control (NAC) determines if a system is sufficiently secure and compliant enough to connect to a network. This is a form of risk-based access control, as systems that are not compliant are considered higher risk and either are placed in a quarantine and remediation network or zone or are prohibited from connecting to the network until they are compliant.
optionNotes: Incorrect. MAC grants access by comparing classification labels on subjects and objects; NAC posture checks evaluate device compliance and health, not security labels.
Correct. NAC posture assessment checks whether a device is secure and compliant enough to connect. Devices that fail are treated as higher risk, so they are quarantined for remediation or blocked.
Incorrect. With DAC, the owner of an object decides who can access it. NAC posture decisions are made automatically by checking a device's compliance, not by an owner's choice.
Incorrect. RBAC grants access based on a user's job role or group membership. Posture assessment looks at an endpoint's security state, such as patches and antivirus, not at roles.

questions.stem: When an application or system allows a logged-in user to perform specific actions, it is an example of what?
questions.explanation: Authorization provides a user with capabilities or rights. Roles and group management are both methods that could be used to match users with rights. Logins are used to validate a user.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Roles are a way of grouping rights so they can be assigned to users. They are a method for granting permissions, not the act of allowing a logged-in user to perform actions.
Incorrect. Group management is a way to match users with rights by putting them into groups. It supports authorization, but it is not the act of granting a user the ability to perform actions.
Incorrect. Logins validate who a user is (authentication). The question describes what a user can do after logging in, so logins don't fit.
Correct. Authorization gives an authenticated user specific capabilities or rights. That matches letting a logged-in user perform specific actions.

questions.stem: Alex has been employed by his company for more than a decade and has held a number of positions in the company. During an audit, it is discovered that he has access to shared folders and applications because of his former roles. What issue has Alex's company encountered?
questions.explanation: Privilege creep occurs when users retain rights they do not need to accomplish their current job from roles they held previously. Unauthorized access occurs when an unauthorized user accesses files. Excessive provisioning is not a term used to describe permissions issues, and account review would help find issues like this.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Excessive provisioning isn't a recognized term for permission problems. Alex's extra rights come from roles he held before, not from being given too much access at setup.
Incorrect. Unauthorized access means someone opens files they aren't authorized to use. Alex's rights were properly granted for earlier roles, and he simply kept them after moving on.
Correct. Privilege creep is when a user keeps rights from earlier roles that their current job doesn't need, which is exactly what the audit found with Alex.
Incorrect. Account review is the control that finds problems like this one. It isn't the problem itself.

questions.stem: Geoff wants to prevent privilege escalation attacks in his organization. Which of the following practices is most likely to prevent horizontal privilege escalation?
options: Limiting permissions for groups and accounts
questions.explanation: Multifactor authentication is most likely to limit horizontal privilege escalation by making it difficult to access user accounts and to authenticate to a compromised account. Limiting permissions for groups and accounts can also help, but disabling unused ports and services and sanitizing user inputs both address threats that are most frequently associated with vertical privilege escalation attacks.
optionNotes: Correct. Horizontal escalation means taking over other accounts at the same privilege level. MFA makes it hard to log in to those accounts, even when a password has been stolen.

Incorrect. Limiting group and account permissions helps somewhat because it reduces what a compromised account can reach. It does not stop an attacker from logging in to peer accounts, so MFA is the better answer.
Incorrect. Disabling unused ports and services shrinks the attack surface. The book links these exploits mostly to vertical escalation (gaining higher privileges), not to taking over peer accounts.
Incorrect. Input sanitization blocks injection and similar application exploits. The book links these mostly to vertical privilege escalation, not to moving across accounts at the same level.

questions.stem: Jim's Microsoft Exchange environment includes servers that are located in local data centers at multiple business offices around the world as well as an Office 365 deployment for employees who are not located at one of those offices. Identities are created and used in both environments and will work in both. What type of federated system is Jim running?
questions.explanation: Hybrid systems use both on-premises and cloud identity and services to provide resources and tools in both environments. While they can be complex, hybrid systems also provide a migration path to a full cloud deployment or for a fault-tolerant design that can handle on-premises or cloud outages while remaining functional.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A cloud-primary federation keeps identity and services mostly in the cloud (e.g., Office 365 alone). Jim also runs on-premises Exchange servers in local data centers, so his setup is not cloud-primary.

Incorrect. An on-premises-primary design keeps identity in local infrastructure and makes little use of the cloud. Here, identities are created and used in Office 365 too, and they work equally in both places.

Correct. A hybrid system uses both on-premises and cloud identity and services, so it provides resources in both environments. That matches Jim's local Exchange servers plus Office 365, with identities that work in both.

Incorrect. Multitenancy means many customers share the same infrastructure, as in a shared data center or cloud. It describes how resources are hosted, not a type of federated identity design spanning on-premises and cloud.

questions.stem:
What type of access control scheme is shown in the following table?
Highly Sensitive Red
Blue
Green
Confidential
Purple Orange Yellow
Internal Use
Black Gray
White
Public
Clear Clear
Clear
questions.explanation: Mandatory access controls (MAC) use a lattice or matrix to describe how classification labels relate to each other. In this image, classification levels are set for each of the labels shown. A discretionary access control (DAC) system would show how the owner of the objects allows access. RBAC could be either rule- or role-based access control and would use either system-wide rules or roles. Task-based access control (TBAC) would list tasks for users.
optionNotes: Incorrect. RBAC (role- or rule-based) grants access through job roles or system-wide rules. The table shows tiers of classification labels, not roles or rules.
Incorrect. In DAC, the object owner decides who gets access. A table of classification levels says nothing about owner-granted permissions.
Correct. MAC uses a lattice of classification labels, such as Highly Sensitive, Confidential, Internal Use and Public, each with its own compartments. That is exactly what the table shows.
Incorrect. TBAC (task-based access control) would list the tasks users are allowed to do. This table lists labels and their classification levels, not tasks.

questions.stem: Michelle's company is creating a new division by splitting the marketing and communications departments into two separate groups. She wants to create roles that provide access to resources used by each group. What should she do to maintain the appropriate security and rights for each group?
options: Put both the marketing and communications teams into the existing group because they will have similar access requirements.
Keep the marketing team in the existing group and create a new communications group based on their specific needs.
Keep the communications' team in the existing group and create a new marketing group based on their specific needs.
Create two new groups, assess which rights they need to perform their roles, and then add additional rights if required.
questions.explanation: Copying existing rights to new groups that have different needs will often result in overly broad privileges. Michelle should create new groups, move all staff into the appropriate groups, and then ensure that they have the access and permissions they need.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Leaving both teams in the existing combined group gives each team access the other team needed. Their needs are no longer the same, so this keeps privileges overly broad and breaks least privilege.

Incorrect. The marketing team would keep the old group's combined rights, including access that only communications needed. Reusing existing rights for a group with different needs leads to overly broad privileges.
Incorrect. This makes the same mistake as B in the other direction. The communications team keeps rights left over from the old combined group, which it may not need, so it ends up over-privileged.

Correct. Creating two new groups, working out what each one actually needs, and adding rights only when required avoids copying broad existing permissions. This follows least privilege and proper role-based access control.

questions.stem: When a subject claims an identity, what process is occurring?
questions.explanation: The process of a subject claiming or professing an identity is known as identification. Authorization verifies the identity of a subject by checking a factor like a password. Logins typically include both identification and authorization, and token presentation is a type of authentication.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A login is a whole process that usually includes both claiming an identity and proving it. It is more than the single step of claiming an identity.
Correct. Identification is when a subject claims or professes an identity, for example by entering a username. Proving that identity comes in a later, separate step.
Incorrect. Authorization happens only after an identity has been claimed. It acts on that claimed identity, so it is not the act of claiming the identity.
Incorrect. Presenting a token is a form of authentication, since it proves an identity that was already claimed. It is not the act of claiming the identity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a common account setting for a service account?
options: Set maximum password age to 90 days.
Set minimum password age to 1 day.
questions.explanation: Service accounts are commonly set to not have expiring passwords to prevent service outages. Organizations may choose to rotate passwords on a regular basis using automation tools as part of their password management strategy to help avoid issues with exposed or compromised service passwords. Disabling complexity requirements and setting a minimum password age are not commonly done for service accounts.
optionNotes: Correct. Service account passwords are usually set to never expire so the services that depend on them don't go down. Rotation is handled separately, often with automation tools.
Incorrect. A 90-day maximum age makes the password expire, and an unexpected expiry can cause a service outage. Expiring passwords is a user-account practice, not a typical service-account setting.
Incorrect. A minimum password age stops users from cycling quickly back to an old password. The book says it is not commonly set for service accounts.
Incorrect. Turning off complexity requirements would weaken a privileged, non-interactive account. The book says this is not a common service-account setting.

questions.stem: Susan's organization is updating its password policy and wants to use the strongest possible passwords. What password requirement will have the highest impact in preventing brute-force attacks?
options: Change the maximum age from 1 year to 180 days.
Increase the minimum password length from 8 characters to 16 characters.
Increase the password complexity so that at least three character classes (such as uppercase, lowercase, numbers, and symbols) are required.
Retain a password history of at least four passwords to prevent reuse.
questions.explanation: Password complexity is driven by length, and a longer password will be more effective against brute-force attacks than a shorter password. Each character of additional length increases the difficulty by the size of the potential character set (for example, a single lowercase character makes the passwords 26 times more difficult to crack). While each of the other settings is useful for a strong password policy, they won't have the same impact on brute-force attacks.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A shorter maximum age only limits how long a cracked password stays usable. It does nothing to make each password harder to brute-force, so the effect is minor compared with adding length.

Correct. Password strength is driven mostly by length. Each extra character multiplies the search space by the size of the character set, so going from 8 to 16 characters makes a brute-force attack vastly harder.

Incorrect. Requiring three character classes enlarges the character set, but the gain is small. Doubling the length grows the search space exponentially and has a far bigger effect on brute-force resistance.
Incorrect. Password history only stops users from reusing old passwords. It does not shrink or expand the keyspace an attacker has to search, so it has little effect on brute-force attacks.

questions.stem: Alaina is performing a regularly scheduled review for service accounts. Which of the following events should she be most concerned about?
options: An interactive login for the service account
A password change for the service account
Limitations placed on the service account's rights
Local use of the service account
questions.explanation: Interactive login for a service account is a critical warning sign, either of compromise or bad administrative practices. In either case, Alaina should immediately work to determine why the account logged in, what occurred, and if the interactive login was done remotely or locally. A remote interactive login for a service account in any professionally maintained environment is an almost guaranteed sign of compromise. Password changes for service accounts may be done as part of ongoing password expiration processes, limitations should always be placed on service accounts rights to ensure that they are only those required, and a local use of the service account as part of the service is a normal event.
optionNotes: Correct. Service accounts should never log in interactively. An interactive login points to compromise or bad admin practice, and a remote one almost certainly means compromise, so it needs investigation right away.
Incorrect. Password changes on service accounts can be part of normal password expiration processes, so on their own they aren't a critical warning sign.
Incorrect. Restricting a service account's rights to only what it needs is least privilege. That's expected good practice, not something to worry about.
Incorrect. A service account being used locally as part of the service it supports is a normal event and doesn't suggest compromise.

questions.stem: When might an organization using biometrics choose to allow a higher FRR instead of a higher FAR?
options: When security is more important than usability
When false rejection is not a concern due to data quality
When the CER of the system is not known
When the CER of the system is very high
questions.explanation: Organizations that have very strict security requirements that don't have a tolerance for false acceptance want to lower the false acceptance rate, or FAR, to be as near to zero as possible. That often means that the false rejection rate, or FRR, increases. Different biometric technologies or a better registration method can help improve biometric performance, but false rejections due to data quality are not typically a concern with modern biometric systems. In this case, knowing the crossover error rate, or CER, or having a very high CER doesn't help the decision.
optionNotes: Correct. When security matters more than convenience, the organization pushes FAR toward zero so impostors are never accepted, and accepts that more legitimate users will be falsely rejected (higher FRR).

Incorrect. Data quality is not what drives this tradeoff. Modern biometric systems don't usually have data-quality false-rejection problems, and better enrollment or a different technology is how you'd address that anyway.

Incorrect. The CER is a metric for comparing the overall accuracy of different devices. Whether or not it's known has no bearing on choosing to favor FRR over FAR, which is a security-versus-usability decision.
Incorrect. A high CER only means the device is less accurate overall. It doesn't tell the organization whether to tune toward false rejections or false acceptances, so it doesn't help the decision.

questions.stem: After recent reports of undesired access to workstations after hours, Derek has been asked to find a way to ensure that maintenance staff cannot log into workstations in business offices. The maintenance staff members do have systems in their break rooms and their offices for the organization, which they still need access to. What should Derek do to meet this need?
options: Require multifactor authentication and allow only office staff to have multifactor tokens.
Use rule-based access control to prevent logins after hours in the business area.
Use role-based access control by setting up a group that contains all maintenance staff and then give that group rights to log into only the designated workstations.
Use geofencing to only allow logins in maintenance areas.
questions.explanation: The most efficient use of Derek's time would be to create a group that is populated with all maintenance staff and then to give that group login rights only to the designated PCs. While time-based constraints might help, in this case, it would continue to allow maintenance staff to log in to PCs that are not intended for use during business hours, leaving a gap in the control. Multifactor authentication, as described, does not meet the requirements of the scenario but may be a good idea overall for greater security for authentication across the organization. Geofencing is typically not accurate enough to rely on inside buildings for specific PCs.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Handing out MFA tokens only to office staff doesn't meet the requirement. Maintenance staff still need to log in to their own systems, and MFA controls how users prove who they are, not which workstations they can use.
Incorrect. A time-based rule against after-hours logins leaves a gap: maintenance staff could still log in to business-office PCs during the day, and those machines aren't meant for them at any hour.

Correct. Putting all maintenance staff in one group and giving that group login rights only to the designated break-room and office PCs blocks access to business workstations while keeping the access they need. It is also the most efficient option to manage.
Incorrect. Geofencing usually isn't accurate enough inside a building to tie logins to specific workstations, so it can't reliably keep maintenance staff off the business-office PCs.

questions.stem: Nick wants to do session management for his web application. Which of the following are common web application session management techniques or methods? (Select all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Common session management techniques include the use of cookies, hidden form fields, URL rewriting, and built-in frameworks like Java's HTTPS session. IP tracking may be included in session information but is not itself a complete session identifier, and TLS token binding is used to make TLS sessions more secure, not to provide session identification.
optionNotes: Incorrect. An IP address can be stored as part of the session information, but it isn't a full session identifier. Many users can share one IP through NAT, and one user's IP can change, so IP tracking isn't a session management method on its own.
Correct. Cookies are the most common way to manage web sessions. They hold a session identifier that the browser sends back with each request. They should only be sent over encrypted channels.
Correct. URL rewriting is a recognized session management technique. It puts the session identifier in the URL, so sessions can be tracked even when the browser doesn't use cookies.
Incorrect. TLS token binding makes TLS sessions more secure by tying tokens to a specific connection. It doesn't identify or manage application sessions.

questions.stem:
For questions 43–45, please use your knowledge of SAML integrations and security architecture design and refer to the following scenario and diagram:
Alex is in charge of SAML integration with a major third-party partner that provides a variety of business productivity services for his organization.
[Figure, described in text: a SAML flow between the Home Organization Identity Provider, the User's web browser and a SAML Integrated Third-Party Service: 1. User attempts to access application. 2. Redirect to SSO URL. 3. Browser accesses SSO URL. 4. Home organization authenticates user and sends SAML response. 5. SAML response sent to browser. 6. Browser sends SAML response to third party. 7. SAML response verified, user logged into third-party application.]

Alex is concerned about eavesdropping on the SAML traffic and also wants to ensure that forged assertions will not be successful. What should he do to prevent these potential attacks?
options: Use SAML's secure mode to provide secure authentication.
Implement TLS using a strong cipher suite, which will protect against both types of attacks.
Implement TLS using a strong cipher suite and use digital signatures.
Implement TLS using a strong cipher suite and message hashing.
questions.explanation: TLS provides message confidentiality and integrity, which can prevent eavesdropping. When paired with digital signatures, which provide integrity and authentication, forged assertions can also be defeated. SAML does not have a security mode and relies on TLS and digital signatures to ensure security if needed. Message hashing without a signature would help prevent modification of the message but won't necessarily provide authentication.
optionNotes: Incorrect. SAML has no "secure mode." For security it relies on outside mechanisms: TLS for the transport and digital signatures on the assertions.
Incorrect. TLS stops eavesdropping in transit, but it does not authenticate where an assertion came from. A forged assertion sent over a valid TLS session would still be accepted unless it is signed.

Correct. TLS gives confidentiality and integrity in transit, which defeats eavesdropping. Digital signatures add integrity and origin authentication to the assertions, so forged assertions are rejected.
Incorrect. A hash without a signature can show that a message was modified, but it doesn't prove who created it. An attacker can forge an assertion and simply compute a matching hash.

questions.stem:
For questions 43–45, please use your knowledge of SAML integrations and security architecture design and refer to the following scenario and diagram:
Alex is in charge of SAML integration with a major third-party partner that provides a variety of business productivity services for his organization.
[Figure, described in text: a SAML flow between the Home Organization Identity Provider, the User's web browser and a SAML Integrated Third-Party Service: 1. User attempts to access application. 2. Redirect to SSO URL. 3. Browser accesses SSO URL. 4. Home organization authenticates user and sends SAML response. 5. SAML response sent to browser. 6. Browser sends SAML response to third party. 7. SAML response verified, user logged into third-party application.]

If Alex's organization is one that is primarily made up of off-site, traveling users, what availability risk does integration of critical business applications to on-site authentication create, and how could he solve it?
options: Third-party integration may not be trustworthy; use SSL and digital signatures.
If the home organization is offline, traveling users won't be able to access third-party applications; implement a hybrid cloud/local authentication system.
Local users may not be properly redirected to the third-party services; implement a local gateway.
Browsers may not properly redirect; use host files to ensure that issues with redirects are resolved.
questions.explanation: Integration with cloud-based third parties that rely on local authentication can fail if the local organization's Internet connectivity or servers are offline. Adopting a hybrid cloud and local authentication system can ensure that Internet or server outages are handled, allowing authentication to work regardless of where the user is or if their home organization is online. Using encrypted and signed communication does not address availability, redirects are a configuration issue with the third party, and a local gateway won't handle remote users. Also, host files don't help with availability issues with services other than DNS.
optionNotes: Incorrect. SSL and digital signatures protect the confidentiality and integrity of SAML exchanges. They do nothing for availability if the home IdP is offline.

Correct. If the on-site IdP or its Internet link goes down, remote users can't authenticate to third-party apps. A hybrid cloud/local authentication setup keeps sign-on working wherever users are and even when the home site is offline.
Incorrect. A local gateway only helps on-site users. This organization is mostly traveling users, and redirect behavior is configured on the third-party side, so this isn't the availability risk.

Incorrect. Hosts files only affect name resolution (the DNS-like lookup). They can't fix an outage of the home organization's authentication servers, and redirects are a third-party configuration issue.

questions.stem:
For questions 43–45, please use your knowledge of SAML integrations and security architecture design and refer to the following scenario and diagram:
Alex is in charge of SAML integration with a major third-party partner that provides a variety of business productivity services for his organization.
[Figure, described in text: a SAML flow between the Home Organization Identity Provider, the User's web browser and a SAML Integrated Third-Party Service: 1. User attempts to access application. 2. Redirect to SSO URL. 3. Browser accesses SSO URL. 4. Home organization authenticates user and sends SAML response. 5. SAML response sent to browser. 6. Browser sends SAML response to third party. 7. SAML response verified, user logged into third-party application.]

What solution can best help address concerns about third parties that control SSO redirects as shown in step 2 in the diagram?
options: An awareness campaign about trusted third parties
Handling redirects at the local site
Implementing an IPS to capture SSO redirect attacks
questions.explanation: While many solutions are technical, if a trusted third party redirects to an unexpected authentication site, awareness is often the best defense. Using TLS would keep the transaction confidential but would not prevent the redirect. Handling redirects locally works only for locally hosted sites, and using a third-party service requires off-site redirects. An IPS might detect an attacker's redirect, but tracking the multitude of load-balanced servers most large providers use can be challenging, if not impossible. In addition, an IPS relies on visibility into the traffic, and SAML integrations should be encrypted for security, which would require a man-in-the-middle type of IPS to be configured.
optionNotes: Correct. Off-site redirects to the third party's SSO URL are unavoidable, so teaching users to recognize trusted partners and spot an unexpected authentication site is often the best defense.
Incorrect. TLS keeps the SAML exchange confidential, but it does nothing to stop a third party, or an attacker, from redirecting users to an unexpected site.
Incorrect. Handling redirects locally only works for sites you host yourself. A third-party service requires redirects to an off-site location.

Incorrect. An IPS needs to see the traffic, but SAML traffic should be encrypted, so the IPS would have to act as a man-in-the-middle. Large providers also spread traffic across many load-balanced servers, which makes redirects hard to track.

questions.stem: Susan has been asked to recommend whether her organization should use a MAC scheme or a DAC scheme. If flexibility and scalability are important requirements for implementing access controls, which scheme should she recommend and why?
options: MAC, because it provides greater scalability and flexibility because you can simply add more labels as needed
DAC, because allowing individual administrators to make choices about the objects they control provides scalability and flexibility
MAC, because compartmentalization is well suited to flexibility and adding compartments will allow it to scale well

DAC, because a central decision process allows quick responses and will provide scalability by reducing the number of decisions required and flexibility by moving those decisions to a central authority
questions.explanation: Discretionary access control (DAC) can provide greater scalability by leveraging many administrators, and those administrators can add flexibility by making decisions about access to their objects without fitting into an inflexible mandatory access control system (MAC). MAC is more secure due to the strong set of controls it provides, but it does not scale as well as DAC and is relatively inflexible in comparison.
optionNotes: Incorrect. MAC is the rigid, centrally enforced label model. Adding labels means policy changes and relabeling every subject and object, so MAC scales worse and is less flexible than DAC, even though it is more secure.

Correct. DAC lets many owners and administrators make access decisions about their own objects. Spreading the work across many people gives scalability, and not being bound to a mandatory label system gives flexibility.
Incorrect. Compartments in MAC enforce need to know through strict labels set by a central authority. That adds rigidity and administrative overhead, so it doesn't make MAC more flexible or scalable.

Incorrect. This describes nondiscretionary access control, where a central authority decides access. DAC puts decisions with the object owners. Central decision-making also creates a bottleneck, which works against both flexibility and scalability.

questions.stem: Which of the following tools is not typically used to verify that a provisioning process was followed in a way that ensures that the organization's security policy is being followed?
questions.explanation: While signature-based detection is used to detect attacks, review of provisioning processes typically involves checking logs, reviewing the audit trail, or performing a manual review of permissions granted during the provisioning process.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Log review is one of the usual ways to confirm provisioning happened correctly. Logs show which accounts were created and which privileges were granted, so you can check them against policy.
Incorrect. Manually reviewing the permissions granted during provisioning checks directly that each account got only the access its approved request and policy allow. It's a normal verification tool.
Correct. Signature-based detection is an IDS/anti-malware method that matches known attack patterns. It finds attacks and doesn't check whether account provisioning followed policy.
Incorrect. Reviewing the audit trail shows who requested, approved and created each account and its privileges. That makes it a standard way to verify the provisioning process was followed.

questions.stem: Jessica wants to adopt an open standard to provide authentication, authorization, and attribute information as part of her cloud identity federation efforts. What standard should she adopt to leverage the flexibility of XML as part of her efforts?
questions.explanation: SAML is an open, XML-based standard used to provide authorization, attribute information, and authentication data. SOAP, or Simple Object Access Protocol, is a messaging protocol and could be used for any XML messaging but is not a markup language itself. OAuth is an authorization framework that exchanges information using APIs, and OpenID Connect is an authentication layer using OAuth that provides both authentication and authorization, but not attribute information.
optionNotes: Correct. SAML is an open XML-based standard that carries authentication assertions, authorization decisions, and attribute information. That makes it the right fit for XML-based identity federation.
Incorrect. SOAP is a messaging protocol that can carry any XML message. It isn't a markup language and doesn't define identity assertions for authentication, authorization, or attributes.
Incorrect. OAuth is an authorization framework that passes information through APIs, usually as tokens, not XML. It doesn't provide authentication or attribute information.

Incorrect. OpenID Connect is an authentication layer built on OAuth that handles authentication and authorization. It doesn't provide the attribute information the question asks for, and it isn't based on XML.

questions.stem: During a penetration test, Chris recovers a file containing hashed passwords for the system he is attempting to access. What type of attack is most likely to succeed against the hashed passwords?
questions.explanation: Rainbow tables are databases of pre-hashed passwords paired with high-speed lookup functions. Since they can quickly compare known hashes against those in a file, using rainbow tables is the fastest way to quickly determine passwords from hashes. A brute-force attack may eventually succeed but will be very slow against most hashes. Pass-the-hash attacks rely on sniffed or otherwise acquired NTLM or LanMan hashes being sent to a system to avoid the need to know a user's password. Salts are data added to a hash to avoid the use of tools like rainbow tables. A salt added to a password means the hash won't match a rainbow table generated without the same salt.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Brute force tries every possible password and hashes each one. It could eventually work, but against most hashes it is very slow, so it is less likely to succeed than a precomputed lookup.
Incorrect. Pass-the-hash sends a captured NTLM or LanMan hash to a system to log in without knowing the password. It does not recover passwords from a file of hashes.
Correct. Rainbow tables are precomputed hash-to-password databases with fast lookup, so they are the quickest way to find passwords from recovered hashes.
Incorrect. A salt is extra data added before hashing to defeat rainbow tables. It is not an attack, and recovering a salt does not crack the passwords by itself.

questions.stem: Google's identity integration with a variety of organizations and applications across domains is an example of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Google's federation with other applications and organizations allows single sign-on as well as management of their electronic identity and its related attributes. While this is an example of SSO, it goes beyond simple single sign-on. Provisioning provides accounts and rights, and a public key infrastructure is used for certificate management.
optionNotes: Incorrect. A public key infrastructure issues and manages digital certificates. It doesn't link identities across organizations and applications.

Correct. Federation shares and manages a user's electronic identity and attributes across domains and organizations. That is what Google's cross-domain identity integration does, and it goes beyond simple SSO.
Incorrect. Google's integration does give users SSO, but SSO is only one benefit. Federation also covers managing the identity and its attributes across organizations, so it is the better answer.
Incorrect. Provisioning is the process of creating accounts and granting rights. It isn't about integrating identities across domains.

questions.stem: Amanda starts at her new job and finds that she has access to a variety of systems that she does not need to accomplish her job. What problem has she encountered?
questions.explanation: When users have more rights than they need to accomplish their job, they have excessive privileges. This is a violation of the concept of least privilege. Unlike privilege creep, this is a provisioning or rights management issue rather than a problem of retention of rights the user needed but no longer requires. Rights collision is a made-up term and thus is not an issue here.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Privilege creep is when someone builds up rights over time and keeps ones they used to need. Amanda is brand new, so this is a provisioning problem, not leftover rights from an earlier role.
Incorrect. 'Rights collision' isn't a real access-management term. It's a made-up distractor and doesn't describe Amanda's situation.
Incorrect. Least privilege is the principle that's being broken here, not the problem itself. Giving her only the access she needs would follow least privilege.
Correct. Amanda has more access than her job requires, which is the definition of excessive privileges. It comes from bad provisioning when she started and violates least privilege.

questions.stem: When Chris verifies an individual's identity and adds a unique identifier like a user ID to an identity system, what process has occurred?
questions.explanation: Registration is the process of adding a user to an identity management system. This includes creating their unique identifier and adding any attribute information that is associated with their identity. Proofing occurs when the user provides information to prove who they are. Directories are managed to maintain lists of users, services, and other items. Session management tracks application and user sessions.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Identity proofing is only the step where the user supplies information proving who they are. Creating the user ID and adding the identity to the system goes beyond proofing.
Correct. Registration adds the user to the identity management system: it creates their unique identifier and attaches their identity attributes, which is exactly what Chris did.
Incorrect. Directory management is the ongoing upkeep of lists of users, services and other objects. It is not the one-time act of verifying a person and creating their identity entry.
Incorrect. Session management tracks active application and user sessions after authentication. It has nothing to do with creating identities.

questions.stem: Selah wants to provide accountability for actions performed via her organization's main line-of-business application. What controls are most frequently used to provide accountability in a situation like this? (Select all that apply.)
options: Provide every staff member with a unique account and enable multifactor authentication.
Enable time- and location-based login requirements.
Provide every staff member with a unique account and require a self-selected password.
questions.explanation: Audit logging when combined with user accounts that can reliably be expected to be accessible only to a specific user due to the use of multifactor authentication is frequently used to provide strong accountability for actions taken via systems and applications. A password can be shared, making it less reliable, and time and location requirements are useful security controls but do not impact accountability.
optionNotes: Correct. Audit logs record which account performed which action. Tied to identities that can be trusted, they supply the evidence that accountability depends on.
Correct. Unique accounts protected by MFA make it reasonably certain that only the assigned person used the account, so logged actions can be reliably attributed to that person.

Incorrect. Time- and location-based login rules are useful access restrictions. However, they only limit when and where someone can log in, not who is accountable, so they do not affect accountability.
Incorrect. Unique accounts help, but a password alone can be shared or stolen. That makes it less reliable for proving that the account owner performed an action.

questions.stem: Charles wants to provide authorization services as part of his web application. What standard should he use if he wants to integrate easily with other web identity providers?
questions.explanation: OAuth is the most widely used open standard for authorization and delegation of rights for cloud services. OpenID is used for authentication, and TACACS+ and RADIUS are primarily used on-site for authentication and authorization for network devices.
optionNotes: Incorrect. OpenID is an authentication standard that proves who a user is. It doesn't handle authorization or delegating access rights, and authorization is what Charles needs.
Incorrect. TACACS+ is a Cisco-developed AAA protocol used mostly on-site to control administrative access to network devices. It isn't a web standard for working with web identity providers.

Incorrect. RADIUS is an AAA protocol used for network access, such as VPN, Wi-Fi and dial-up, mostly in on-site environments. It isn't designed to integrate web applications with web identity providers.
Correct. OAuth is the most widely used open standard for authorization and for delegating access rights across web and cloud services. Major web identity providers support it, so integration is easy.

questions.stem: The company that Cameron works for uses a system that allows users to request privileged access to systems when necessary. Cameron requests access, and the request is pre-approved due to his role. He is then able to access the system to perform the task. Once he is done, the rights are removed. What type of system is he using?
questions.explanation: Cameron is using a just-in-time (JIT) system that provides the access needed when it is needed. A zero trust system requires authentication and authorization when actions are performed but does not necessarily require privileges to be granted and removed when they are needed.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Zero trust demands authentication and authorization for every action. It doesn't inherently grant privileges on request and then strip them once the task is done.
Incorrect. Federated identity management extends SSO across organizations (for example, by using SAML). It's about sharing identities, not about temporarily granting and revoking privileged rights.
Incorrect. With SSO, a user authenticates once and can then reach multiple resources. It's a convenience feature for authentication and doesn't grant or remove privileges as needed.
Correct. Just-in-time access grants privileged rights only when they're requested (here, pre-approved based on Cameron's role) and removes them once the task is finished.

questions.stem: Elle is responsible for building a banking website. She needs proof of the identity of the users who register for the site. How should she validate user identities?
options: Require users to create unique questions that only they will know.
Require new users to bring their driver's license or passport in person to the bank.
Use information that both the bank and the user have such as questions pulled from their credit report.
Call the user on their registered phone number to verify that they are who they claim to be.
questions.explanation: Identity proofing can be done by comparing user information that the organization already has, like account numbers or personal information. Requiring users to create unique questions can help with future support by providing a way for them to do password resets. Using a phone call only verifies that the individual who created the account has the phone that they registered and won't prove their identity. In-person verification would not fit the business needs of most websites.
optionNotes: Incorrect. User-created secret questions don't prove who someone is at registration, because the user makes them up. They are useful later as a support mechanism, such as for password resets.

Incorrect. Checking a passport or driver's license in person is valid identity proofing, as is done for new employees. However, it doesn't fit the business needs of a website where users register online.

Correct. Identity proofing compares information the organization already has, such as credit-report-based knowledge questions or account details, with what the claimed user knows. This works well for remote online registration.
Incorrect. A call to the registered phone number only shows that whoever created the account has that phone. It doesn't prove the person's real identity.

questions.stem: Susan's organization is part of a federation that allows users from multiple organizations to access resources and services at other federated sites. When Susan wants to use a service at a partner site, which identity provider is used?
options: Both their identity provider and the service provider's identity provider.
The service provider creates a new identity.
questions.explanation: In federated systems, a user's access to services is authenticated through their own organization's identity provider (IDP). Service providers query those IDPs when the user attempts to authenticate to the service and, if the request is validated, allow access based on the rules and policies set for the service based on attributes that may be relevant that are provided by the IDP.
optionNotes: Correct. In a federation the user authenticates through their own home organization's IdP. The service provider trusts that IdP's assertion and grants access according to its own policies, using the attributes the IdP supplies.

Incorrect. The service provider doesn't authenticate federated users itself. It sends them to their home IdP and relies on the assertion that comes back. Avoiding separate identities at each partner is the whole point of federation.
Incorrect. Only one IdP is involved: the user's home IdP. The service provider queries that IdP and then makes its own authorization decision, so there is no second authentication by an SP-side IdP.
Incorrect. Creating a new identity at each partner site is the separate-account model that federation replaces. Federation reuses the home identity and passes its attributes to the service provider.

questions.stem: A new customer at a bank that uses fingerprint scanners to authenticate its users is surprised when he scans his fingerprint and is logged into another customer's account. What type of biometric factor error occurred?
options: A time of use, method of use error
questions.explanation: Type 2 errors occur in biometric systems when an invalid subject is incorrectly authenticated as a valid user. In this case, nobody except the actual customer should be validated when fingerprints are scanned. Type 1 errors occur when a valid subject is not authenticated; if the existing customer is rejected, it is a Type 1 error. Registration is the process of adding users, but registration errors and time of use, method of use errors are not specific biometric authentication terms.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Registration (enrollment) is how users get added to the system, but "registration error" isn't a standard biometric error term. The problem here is a false acceptance, not an enrollment failure.
Incorrect. A Type 1 error (false rejection) happens when a valid user is wrongly denied. Here the system let in the wrong person, which is the opposite problem.
Correct. A Type 2 error (false acceptance) is when an invalid subject is authenticated as a valid user. That is what happened when the new customer's fingerprint opened another customer's account.
Incorrect. "Time of use, method of use" is not a biometric authentication error term. It sounds like TOCTOU, which is a race-condition attack, not a biometric accuracy measure.

questions.stem: What type of access control is typically used by firewalls?
questions.explanation: Firewalls use rule-based access control, or Rule-BAC, in their access control lists and apply rules created by administrators to all traffic that passes through them. DAC, or discretionary access control, allows owners to determine who can access objects they control, while task-based access control lists tasks for users. MAC, or mandatory access control, uses classifications to determine access.
optionNotes: Incorrect. DAC lets object owners decide who can access the resources they control. A firewall works differently: administrators set the rules and those rules apply to all traffic, so owner discretion doesn't come into it.
Correct. Firewalls use rule-based access control (Rule-BAC). Administrators write rules into ACLs, and the firewall applies those rules to every packet that passes through it.
Incorrect. Task-based access control grants access based on the tasks assigned to users. Firewalls filter traffic against ACL rules, not against user tasks.
Incorrect. MAC decides access by comparing classification labels on subjects and objects. Firewalls match traffic against administrator-written rules, not security labels.

questions.stem: When you input a user ID and password, you are performing what important identity and access management activity?
questions.explanation: When you input a username and password, you are authenticating yourself by providing a unique identifier and a verification that you are the person who should have that identifier (the password). Authorization is the process of determining what a user is allowed to do. Validation and login both describe elements of what is happening in the process; however, they aren't the most important identity and access management activity.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Authorization comes after authentication and decides what an authenticated user is allowed to do. Typing in credentials doesn't grant any permissions.
Incorrect. Validation describes part of what happens when credentials are checked, but it isn't the formal IAM activity the question is asking for.
Correct. Entering a user ID (the claimed identity) together with a password (the proof) is authentication: it verifies that you are the person who holds that identifier.
Incorrect. Login is the everyday name for the process. It describes the mechanics, not the core IAM activity, which is authentication.

questions.stem: Kathleen works for a data center hosting facility that provides physical data center space for individuals and organizations. Until recently, each client was given a magnetic-strip-based keycard to access the section of the facility where their servers are located, and they were also given a key to access the cage or rack where their servers reside. In the past month, a number of servers have been stolen, but the logs for the passcards show only valid IDs. What is Kathleen's best option to make sure that the users of the passcards are who they are supposed to be?
options: Add a reader that requires a PIN for passcard users.
Add a camera system to the facility to observe who is accessing servers.
Replace the magnetic stripe keycards with smartcards.
questions.explanation: Kathleen should implement a biometric factor. The cards and keys are an example of a Type 2 factor, or “something you have.” Using a smart card replaces this with another Type 2 factor, but the cards could still be loaned out or stolen. Adding a PIN would address the problem by adding a second authentication factor, but PINs may be written down and are prone to theft or even guessing for shorter PINs, so a biometric factor is preferable if it is available. Adding cameras doesn't prevent access to the facility and thus doesn't solve the immediate problem (but it is a good idea!).
optionNotes: Incorrect. A PIN does add a second factor (something you know), but PINs can be written down, stolen, shared, or guessed if short. So it ties the card to the right person less reliably than a biometric.
Incorrect. Cameras are a detective control. They record who goes in but don't stop anyone from getting in, so they don't fix the immediate problem of cardholders not being who they claim to be.

Correct. A biometric adds something you are (Type 3) on top of the card (Type 2). It can't easily be loaned out, written down, or stolen, so it best confirms that the person holding the card is the authorized user.
Incorrect. A smartcard is still just something you have (Type 2), the same kind of factor as the magnetic-stripe card. It can still be loaned out or stolen, so it doesn't prove who is holding it.

questions.stem: Theresa wants to allow her staff to securely store and manage passwords for systems including service accounts and other rarely used administrative credentials. What type of tool should she implement to enable this?
questions.explanation: Enterprise credential management tools, often called password vaults, allow passwords to be securely generated, stored, and managed. They can provide logs of who uses passwords, when they were updated, and if they meet complexity and other requirements. Of course, this means the keys to your environment are all in one place, so securing and managing the enterprise password manager is very important!
optionNotes: Incorrect. Single sign-on lets a user log in once and reach many systems in one organization. It doesn't store or manage separate shared credentials like service account and rarely used admin passwords.

Incorrect. Federated identity management builds trust relationships so one login works across organizations. It handles authentication between parties, not secure storage and management of service or admin account passwords.

Correct. A password vault (enterprise credential manager) securely generates, stores and manages passwords. It also logs who used each password and when it was updated, and checks complexity, so it fits service and rarely used admin credentials.
Incorrect. Multifactor authentication makes logins stronger by requiring more than one factor. It doesn't give staff a secure place to store and manage the passwords for service and admin accounts.

questions.stem: Olivia wants to limit the commands that a user can run via sudo to limit the potential for privilege escalation attacks. What Linux file should she modify to allow this?
questions.explanation: The sudoers file can list the specific users who can use sudo as well as the commands or directories that are allowed for them.
optionNotes: Incorrect. Bash has no ".bin" configuration file that controls sudo. Bash startup files like .bashrc only set up the shell environment, so they can't stop a user from running privileged commands through sudo.
Correct. The sudoers file (/etc/sudoers, edited with visudo) lists which users can use sudo and which specific commands or directories each one is allowed, which limits privilege escalation.
Incorrect. There is no ".allowed" bash configuration file. Sudo permissions are granted through the sudoers file, not through shell configuration files.
Incorrect. "sudont" is a made-up distractor, not a real Linux file. Both allowing and restricting sudo commands are done in the sudoers file.

questions.stem: Which objects and subjects have a label in a MAC model?
options: Objects and subjects that are classified as Confidential, Secret, or Top Secret have a label.
All objects have a label, and all subjects have a compartment.
All objects and subjects have a label.
All subjects have a label and all objects have a compartment.
questions.explanation: In a mandatory access control system, all subjects and objects have a label. Compartments may or may not be used, but there is not a specific requirement for either subjects or objects to be compartmentalized. The specific labels of Confidential, Secret, and Top Secret are not required by MAC.
optionNotes: Incorrect. MAC labels every subject and object, not just ones at certain levels. It also doesn't require the government levels Confidential, Secret, and Top Secret; any labeling scheme works, and unclassified items still carry a label.
Incorrect. Objects do get labels, but subjects get them too. Compartments are optional in MAC, so subjects aren't required to have one.
Correct. In mandatory access control, every subject and every object carries a label. The system compares those labels to make access decisions.
Incorrect. Subjects do get labels, but objects need labels too. Compartments are optional in MAC and can't stand in for labels on objects.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
Chris is the identity architect for a growing e-commerce website that wants to leverage social identity. To do this, he and his team intend to allow users to use their existing Google accounts as their primary accounts when using the e-commerce site. This means that when a new user initially connects to the e-commerce platform, they are given the choice between using their Google account using OAuth 2.0 or creating a new account on the platform using their own email address and a password of their choice.
[Figure, described in text: an OAuth flow between the Client, the E-commerce Application Servers and Google Servers: 1. Anti-forgery token created. 2. User login and consent to data release. 3. Token confirmed and authorization code sent. 4. Exchange code for access and ID token. 5. Token response. 6. Call Google API using token.]

When the e-commerce application creates an account for a Google user, where should that user's password be stored?
options: The password is stored in the e-commerce application's database.
The password is stored in memory on the e-commerce application's server.
The password is stored in Google's account management system.
The password is never stored; instead, a salted hash is stored in Google's account management system.
questions.explanation: Passwords are never stored for web applications in a well-designed environment. Instead, salted hashes are stored and compared to passwords after they are salted and hashed. If the hashes match, the user is authenticated.
optionNotes: Incorrect. With OAuth the e-commerce site never receives the Google user's password; it gets only tokens. A well-designed system also never stores plaintext passwords, it stores salted hashes.
Incorrect. Keeping the password in server memory still means storing a plaintext credential the relying party should never have. With OAuth, the user types the password only into Google's login page.

Incorrect. This picks the right location, Google, but the wrong form. Well-designed systems keep a salted hash and compare it against the salted hash of whatever password is entered, not the password itself.
Correct. Google authenticates the user, and well-designed systems never store the actual password. They store a salted hash and compare it to the salted hash of the password entered at login.

questions.stem:
Scenario:
Chris is the identity architect for a growing e-commerce website that wants to leverage social identity. To do this, he and his team intend to allow users to use their existing Google accounts as their primary accounts when using the e-commerce site. This means that when a new user initially connects to the e-commerce platform, they are given the choice between using their Google account using OAuth 2.0 or creating a new account on the platform using their own email address and a password of their choice.
[Figure, described in text: an OAuth flow between the Client, the E-commerce Application Servers and Google Servers: 1. Anti-forgery token created. 2. User login and consent to data release. 3. Token confirmed and authorization code sent. 4. Exchange code for access and ID token. 5. Token response. 6. Call Google API using token.]

Which of the following is responsible for user authentication for Google users?
options: Both the e-commerce application and Google servers.
The diagram does not provide enough information to determine this.
questions.explanation: When a third-party site integrates via OAuth 2.0, authentication is handled by the service provider's servers. In this case, Google is acting as the service provider for user authentication. Authentication for local users who create their own accounts would occur in the e-commerce application (or a related server), but that is not the question that is asked here.
optionNotes: Incorrect. The e-commerce app only authenticates local users who made their own email/password accounts. For Google users, it receives tokens from Google and never checks their credentials itself.
Incorrect. Authentication isn't shared here. In OAuth 2.0 the user logs in and gives consent on Google's servers (step 2), and the e-commerce app just trades the authorization code for tokens.

Correct. With OAuth 2.0 social login, the identity provider's servers handle authentication, and here that is Google. The user logs in to Google, and Google sends an authorization code and ID token back to the site.

Incorrect. There is enough information. The flow shows the user logging in and consenting on Google's servers, which is the usual OAuth social login pattern (like using 'Log in with Google' on a site Google doesn't own).
